June 9, 2026 
 
Mehmet Oz, MD, MBA 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
200 Independence Avenue, SW 
Washington, DC 20201 
 
Thomas Keane, MD, MBA 
National Coordinator for Health Information Technology 
Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology 
330 C Street SW 
Washington, DC 20201 
 
Submitted electronically via www.regulations.gov   
  
Re: Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule 
 
Dear Administrator Oz and Coordinator Keane: 
 
Oncology nurses are privileged to support people with cancer through their entire cancer experience, from 
diagnosis and treatment into survivorship or as they face their end-of-life journey. On behalf of the Oncology 
Nursing Society (ONS), which represents more than 100,000 oncology nurses nationwide, we appreciate the 
opportunity to comment on the aforementioned proposed rule.  
General Comments 
ONS supports efforts by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) and the Office of the National 
Coordinator for Health IT (ONC) to modernize prior authorization processes, expand interoperability, and 
improve transparency. Specifically, we support proposals that would require impacted payers to support 
electronic prior authorization and make decisions within shorter, aligned timeframes across CMS programs, 
as well as increase transparency for the prior authorization of drugs by requiring denial reasons and reporting 
on key metrics. We also support requirements for impacted payers to update health information technology 
(health IT) standards, report interoperability API endpoints and usage metrics to CMS, and adopt Health Level 
SevenÂ® (HL7Â®) Fast Healthcare Interoperability ResourcesÂ® (FHIRÂ®) standards and implementation 
specifications for prior authorization transactions across HIPAA-covered entities.  
 
In the sections that follow, we provide feedback on specific sections of the proposed rule as they pertain to 
cancer care and treatment. 
Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs 
ONS supports proposals that would require impacted payers to incorporate coverage and 
documentation requirements into the Prior Authorization API to support electronic prior authorization 
for drugs covered under a medical benefit beginning October 1, 2027. However, we are concerned that 
the proposed framework does not adequately address medications that may be covered under either 
 
 
the medical or pharmacy benefit depending on formulation, route of administration, site of care, or 
other variations in payer benefit design and utilization management policies.
 
This issue is particularly significant in oncology, where many therapies and supportive care medications 
may exist in multiple formulations or delivery pathways. Cancer treatments may be available as infused 
therapies covered under the medical benefit as well as oral, self-administered, or subcutaneous 
formulations covered under the pharmacy benefit. In addition, payer policies related to specialty 
pharmacy distribution, white bagging arrangements, and site-of-care restrictions may further shift drugs 
between benefit structures.
 
Oncology nurses are deeply involved in navigating these coverage pathways, obtaining prior 
authorizations, coordinating treatment access, and resolving payer-related barriers to care. Despite 
these realities, there is currently no unified standard or mechanism that allows oncology clinicians to 
view coverage requirements, prior authorization criteria, step therapy protocols, and related 
documentation requirements for all formulations of a medication in a single, integrated workflow. 
Instead, oncology clinicians are forced to navigate separate medical and pharmacy benefit systems to 
determine coverage pathways, prior authorization requirements, and utilization management criteria 
for the same medication depending on formulation, route of administration, site of care, or other payer 
benefit design variations.
 
This fragmentation perpetuates administrative burden for oncology nurses and care teams, who are 
often responsible for coordinating treatment access and resolving payer-related barriers while patients 
await medically necessary cancer care. ONS encourages CMS and ONC to work with industry 
stakeholders to close this gap and develop a more seamless interoperability framework that supports 
consolidated access to coverage and documentation requirements across all formulations and benefit 
structures associated with a medication. Providers, oncology nurses, and patients should be able to 
access this information through a unified process that promotes timely treatment decisions, continuity 
of care, and reduced administrative complexity.
Improving Communications and Decision Timeframes for Prior Authorizations 
ONS supports the proposal that state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid managed care plans, 
CHIP managed care entities, and QHP issuers on the FFEs would be required to provide providers with a 
specific reason for denying a prior authorization request for drugs, regardless of the method used to 
submit the request or communicate the decision, beginning October 1, 2027. Improved transparency 
regarding prior authorization denials is critical to helping oncology providers and nurses more efficiently 
address coverage barriers and avoid unnecessary delays in care.
 
ONS also supports proposals requiring Medicare Advantage (MA) organizations to publicly report prior 
authorization metrics related to drugs payable under Part B, and requiring state Medicaid and CHIP FFS 
programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and QHP issuers on the FFEs to 
publicly report prior authorization metrics for drugs beginning in 2028 using data from the 2027 
reporting period. In addition, CMS should include cancer drugs payable under Part A, particularly 
where prior authorization requirements may apply in connection with inpatient or bundled oncology 
services, to provide a complete picture of the real-world impact of prior authorization on cancer care.
 
Further, ONS believes all impacted payers should be required to adhere to a 24-hour prior 
authorization decision timeframe for cancer drugs regardless of whether the therapy is covered under 
the medical or pharmacy benefit. Cancer treatment is inherently time-sensitive, and patients facing a 
 
 
cancer diagnosis should not experience unnecessary delays while awaiting coverage determinations. 
Oncology providers and nurses already follow evidence-based clinical pathways and guideline-driven 
treatment protocols designed to support appropriate therapy selection. Delays beyond 24 hours can 
contribute to patient anxiety, disrupt treatment planning, and potentially delay initiation of medically 
necessary care.
Updates to Patient Access, Provider Directory, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs; 
API Usage Metrics 
ONS supports ONCâ€™s proposal to require impacted payers to add information about prior authorization 
requests and decisions for all drugs to the categories of data required to be made available through the 
Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs (â€œAccess APIsâ€) by October 1, 2027, within the 
same timeframes established for non-drug items and services. ONS also supports proposals requiring 
Medicaid managed care plans and CHIP managed care entities to report Patient Access API usage 
metrics to the state, by program and plan, and requiring QHP issuers on the FFEs to report Patient 
Access API usage metrics to CMS. In addition, ONS supports proposals requiring impacted payers to 
report aggregated, de-identified metrics regarding use of the Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, and Prior 
Authorization APIs beginning in 2028 using data from the 2027 reporting period.
 
However, ONS opposes the proposal to remove drug formulary information from the Provider Access 
and Payer-to-Payer APIs for MA organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid 
managed care plans, and CHIP managed care entities. As discussed above, oncology nurses frequently 
rely on coverage, utilization management, and formulary information to coordinate timely access to 
cancer therapies and supportive care medications, particularly for patients transitioning between payers 
during active treatment and for medications that may shift between the medical and pharmacy benefit 
depending on formulation, route of administration, site of care, or other payer benefit design variations. 
Removing formulary information from these APIs would eliminate an important opportunity to advance 
more integrated and interoperable access to coverage and utilization management information across 
payers. While a seamless process for accessing this information does not currently exist, retaining 
formulary data within these APIs could help support future interoperability efforts intended to reduce 
fragmented workflows and administrative burden associated with navigating separate medical and 
pharmacy benefit systems. As such, ONS encourages ONC to retain formulary information within these 
APIs and continue working with stakeholders to improve the standardization and usability of 
formulary and utilization management data across payers.
Requests for Information 
Step Therapy 
ONS appreciates the focus on improving step therapy processes through technology and data sharing, 
including through the Payer-to-Payer API. For patients with cancer, delays or redundant step therapy 
requirements can result in missed treatment windows, disease progression, increased symptom burden, 
and diminished quality of life. We agree that interoperability across systems has the potential to reduce 
administrative burden and improve continuity of care, particularly when patients transition between 
payers during active cancer care and treatment. However, meaningful streamlining of step therapy 
processes will be difficult to achieve without more integrated access to coverage, formulary, and 
utilization management information across both the medical and pharmacy benefit. As discussed 
above, oncology therapies and supportive care medications may shift between benefit structures 
depending on formulation, route of administration, site of care, specialty pharmacy distribution 
arrangements, or other payer benefit design variations. Because step therapy requirements are often 
 
 
directly tied to formulary placement and utilization management protocols, oncology nurses are forced 
to navigate separate medical and pharmacy benefit systems to determine whether a patient has already 
satisfied prior step therapy requirements or whether a therapy remains subject to additional utilization 
management criteria.
 
ONS strongly encourages CMS and ONC to work with stakeholders to support more seamless 
interoperability between medical and pharmacy benefit systems so that technology can more 
effectively facilitate step therapy determinations, continuity of care, and recognition of prior payer 
determinations. Payers should use available claims, encounter, and clinical data to recognize and honor 
previously completed step therapy requirements unless there is a clear, documented clinical rationale to 
require additional steps. ONS encourages CMS to ensure that interoperability efforts support continuity 
of care by facilitating the transfer and recognition of prior step therapy determinations when patients 
transition between health plans. Patients should not be required to repeat step therapy protocols, 
restart utilization management processes, or undergo non-medical treatment changes solely because of 
a coverage transition, particularly during active cancer treatment. Requiring patients with cancer to 
repeat step therapy requirements after changing health plans, particularly where prior therapies were 
ineffective or poorly tolerated, offers little clinical value and can delay medically necessary treatment. 
ONS also encourages CMS to support greater transparency into guideline-aligned step therapy 
criteria, exception processes, and utilization management protocols at the point of care, particularly in 
oncology where treatment decisions depend on prior lines of therapy, molecular profiling, rapidly 
evolving clinical guidelines, and patient-specific factors.
 
At the same time, ONS encourages CMS and ONC to maintain appropriate guardrails around the use of 
automation in utilization management processes. Technology should be used to facilitate 
administrative processes, such as identifying documentation requirements or retrieving historical 
treatment information, but should not replace clinician judgment in complex oncology care decisions. 
Human clinical review remains essential for therapies involving significant toxicity, narrow therapeutic 
windows, or curative intent. ONS also encourages CMS to evaluate step therapy policies using patient-
centered measures, including treatment delays, therapy abandonment, disease progression risk, and 
administrative burden on patients and oncology care teams, rather than relying solely on cost or 
utilization metrics.  
Laboratory Tests and Durable Medical Equipment, Prosthetics, Orthotics, and Supplies (DMEPOS) Items  
ONS appreciates CMSâ€™ focus on the impact of prior authorization requirements for laboratory tests on 
patient care and provider burden. In oncology, timely access to molecular diagnostics, biomarker 
testing, genetic testing, and other laboratory services is critical to diagnosis, treatment selection, 
monitoring treatment response, and determining whether patients can safely proceed with therapy. 
Delays associated with prior authorization can postpone medically necessary cancer care and create 
significant administrative burden for oncology nurses, who are often responsible for coordinating 
testing, tracking approvals, and helping patients navigate coverage barriers. ONS also recognizes the 
importance of appropriate clinician involvement and evidence-based use of advanced laboratory testing, 
particularly for emerging technologies and high-cost diagnostics where clinical utility, regulatory status, 
or guideline support may still be evolving.
 
ONS also emphasizes the importance of timely access to DMEPOS items for patients with cancer, 
including compression garments covered under the Lymphedema Treatment Act, home feeding supplies, 
mobility aids (walkers and wheelchairs), home infusion equipment, oxygen, wound care supplies, 
suction set ups, and tracheostomy care items. These supportive care items are often essential to 
 
 
symptom management, recovery, safe discharge from the hospital, and a patientâ€™s ability to tolerate and 
adhere to cancer treatment. Delays associated with prior authorization can contribute to patient 
anxiety, clinical deterioration, avoidable delays in hospital discharge or treatment, as well as increased 
healthcare utilization and costs, and added financial stress for patients. Oncology nurses and providers 
frequently absorb the administrative burden associated with navigating these requirements, diverting 
time from direct patient care to paperwork, peer-to-peer reviews, and appeals.
 
For these reasons, ONS encourages CMS and ONC to work with stakeholders to streamline prior 
authorization requirements for oncology-related laboratory tests and DMEPOS items, reduce 
redundant documentation requirements, and leverage interoperability and automation tools to 
improve coordination among providers, laboratories, suppliers, and payers while continuing to 
support clinically appropriate utilization and informed decision-making for complex oncology-related 
laboratory services.
 
 
*** 
 
We appreciate your consideration of these important issues as CMS and ONC finalize these proposals. ONS 
stands ready to provide oncology nursing expertise and serve as a resource as these efforts move forward. If 
you have any questions or would like to discuss these comments in more detail, please contact us at 
healthpolicy@ons.org. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
The Oncology Nursing Society 
 
The Oncology Nursing Society (ONS) is a professional association that represents 100,000 nurses and is the 
professional home to more than 35,000 members. ONS is committed to promoting excellence in oncology 
nursing and the transformation of cancer care. Since 1975, ONS has provided a professional community for 
oncology nurses, developed evidence-based education programs and treatment information, and advocated 
for patient care, all in an effort to improve the quality of life and outcomes for patients with cancer and their 
families.

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** The Oncology Nursing Society (ONS)
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association / Healthcare Provider
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Represents more than 100,000 oncology nurses nationwide and is the professional home to more than 35,000 members; provides oncology nursing education, treatment information, and patient-care advocacy.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

ONS supports CMS and ONC efforts to modernize prior authorization, improve transparency, update health IT standards, report API endpoints and usage metrics, and adopt HL7 FHIR standards for prior authorization transactions. Its main modification requests are to close gaps between medical and pharmacy benefit workflows, require 24-hour PA decisions for cancer drugs, retain formulary information in Access APIs, streamline step therapy, and extend interoperability improvements to oncology-related laboratory tests and DMEPOS.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** Not addressed by CFR citation.
- **Standards referenced:** HL7 FHIR; Prior Authorization API; Patient Access API; Provider Access API; Payer-to-Payer API; Provider Directory API; health IT standards; implementation specifications.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs Across Benefit Structures**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL / PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Oncology therapies and supportive medications may move between medical and pharmacy benefits based on formulation, route, site of care, specialty pharmacy distribution, white bagging, and payer design.
- **Specific request:** Develop a seamless interoperability framework that gives clinicians consolidated access to coverage, documentation, PA criteria, step therapy, and utilization management requirements across formulations and benefit structures.

**Topic 2: Denial Reasons, Metrics, and Cancer Drug Timeframes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS / PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS / API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Specific denial reasons and public metrics help oncology teams address coverage barriers; cancer treatment is time-sensitive and delays can disrupt treatment planning.
- **Specific request:** Require specific denial reasons, public PA metrics, inclusion of Part A cancer drugs where PA applies, and a 24-hour PA decision timeframe for cancer drugs regardless of benefit category.

**Topic 3: Access APIs and Formulary Information**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED / API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support / Oppose
- **Rationale:** ONS supports adding drug PA requests and decisions to Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs and reporting aggregated de-identified API metrics, but formulary data is essential for oncology care coordination.
- **Specific request:** Retain drug formulary information in the Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs and improve standardization and usability of formulary and utilization management data.

**Topic 4: Step Therapy Continuity and Automation Guardrails**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Repeated step therapy after a payer transition can delay medically necessary cancer care, while automation should not replace clinician judgment in complex oncology decisions.
- **Specific request:** Use claims, encounter, and clinical data to recognize prior step therapy determinations; provide transparent guideline-aligned criteria and exception processes; maintain human clinical review for complex oncology care.

**Topic 5: Laboratory Tests and DMEPOS**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Molecular diagnostics, biomarker testing, genetic testing, DMEPOS, and supportive-care supplies are essential to diagnosis, treatment selection, discharge, recovery, and treatment adherence in oncology.
- **Specific request:** Streamline PA for oncology-related labs and DMEPOS, reduce redundant documentation, and improve coordination among providers, laboratories, suppliers, and payers.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12:** ONS identifies a technical/workflow challenge for drug PA: medical and pharmacy benefit systems are fragmented and do not provide unified access to requirements for all formulations of a medication.
- **S15:** ONS directly addresses the medical-versus-pharmacy distinction and asks CMS/ONC to support consolidated benefit-spanning information for oncology medications.
- **S16:** ONS supports requiring specific reasons for drug PA denials so oncology providers can resolve barriers and avoid delays.
- **S20:** ONS asks CMS to require a 24-hour decision timeframe for cancer drugs regardless of whether the drug is covered under the medical or pharmacy benefit.
- **S21:** ONS supports the October 1, 2027 implementation date for medical-benefit drug ePA but asks for policies that address cross-benefit realities.
- **S23-S24:** ONS supports reporting API endpoints and technical information to CMS, although it does not propose detailed endpoint-reporting content.
- **S29-S35:** ONS supports Patient Access API usage reporting and aggregated, de-identified metrics for Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, and Prior Authorization APIs beginning with 2027 data reported in 2028; it also requests cancer Part A drug PA metrics.
- **S37:** ONS describes implementation challenges caused by fragmented oncology benefit structures, formulary data gaps, and utilization management workflows.
- **S44-S45:** ONS supports adopting HL7 FHIR standards and implementation specifications for prior authorization transactions across HIPAA-covered entities.
- **S66-S82:** ONS responds to general RFIs on step therapy, laboratory tests, and DMEPOS by urging continuity of prior determinations, transparency, automation guardrails, and streamlined PA processes.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize requirements for electronic prior authorization for medical-benefit drugs.
2. Develop a unified framework for coverage and documentation requirements across medical and pharmacy benefit structures.
3. Require specific reasons for drug PA denials across affected Medicaid, CHIP, and QHP entities.
4. Publicly report PA metrics for drugs and include Part A cancer drugs where PA applies.
5. Require all impacted payers to meet a 24-hour PA decision timeframe for cancer drugs.
6. Add drug PA request and decision information to Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs.
7. Retain formulary information in Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs.
8. Use interoperability to recognize prior step therapy determinations when patients change plans.
9. Preserve clinician judgment and human review for complex oncology utilization management.
10. Streamline PA and reduce redundant documentation for oncology laboratory tests and DMEPOS.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Fragmented medical/pharmacy benefit systems, lack of unified coverage information, cancer treatment delays, removal of formulary data from APIs, repeated step therapy, and PA barriers for labs and DMEPOS.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Missed treatment windows, disease progression, increased symptom burden, diminished quality of life, patient anxiety, delayed discharge or treatment, added financial stress, and diverted nursing time.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Separate benefit systems, inconsistent payer policies, specialty pharmacy and white-bagging arrangements, site-of-care restrictions, formulary data gaps, and redundant documentation requirements.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** ONS represents more than 100,000 oncology nurses and more than 35,000 members.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Not addressed.
- **Examples provided:** Infused versus oral or subcutaneous cancer therapies; specialty pharmacy distribution; white bagging; site-of-care restrictions; repeated step therapy after payer transitions; molecular diagnostics, biomarker testing, genetic testing, compression garments, feeding supplies, mobility aids, oxygen, wound care, suction setups, and tracheostomy supplies.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Patients with cancer, oncology nurses, oncology providers, payers, pharmacies, laboratories, suppliers, states, QHP issuers, MA organizations, and health IT stakeholders.
- **Economic implications:** ONS does not quantify costs but links delays and redundant PA work to increased utilization, avoidable administrative burden, and patient financial stress.
- **Technical feasibility:** ONS views interoperability as necessary and beneficial but incomplete unless standards support cross-benefit formulary, coverage, PA, step therapy, and utilization management data.
- **Patient care impact:** High; recommended changes would support faster treatment decisions, continuity of care, safer discharge, reduced delays, and better access to cancer therapies and supportive services.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Mixed
- **Tone:** Professional, technical, collaborative
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "ONS supports efforts ... to modernize prior authorization processes, expand interoperability, and improve transparency." - Context: Overall support for the proposed rule.
2. "there is currently no unified standard or mechanism" - Context: ONS's central concern about fragmented medical and pharmacy benefit workflows.
3. "all impacted payers should be required to adhere to a 24-hour prior authorization decision timeframe for cancer drugs" - Context: Recommended cancer-drug PA timeframe.
4. "Technology should be used to facilitate administrative processes ... but should not replace clinician judgment" - Context: Guardrails for automation in oncology utilization management.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - ONS supports October 1, 2027 and 2028 reporting dates while emphasizing time-sensitive cancer care and 24-hour decisions.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - The comment repeatedly describes administrative burden on oncology nurses and care teams.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - ONS supports FHIR/API-based exchange but says current fragmented systems need more integrated cross-benefit functionality.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - ONS supports HL7 FHIR adoption and asks for better standardization of formulary and utilization management data.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - The comment centers on timely cancer therapy, diagnostics, DMEPOS, and supportive care access.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - ONS asks CMS and ONC to work with industry stakeholders, providers, laboratories, suppliers, and payers.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - This is one of the comment's core themes, especially for oncology drugs with multiple formulations.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - ONS supports denial reasons, public metrics, formulary data retention, and transparent step therapy criteria.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - The comment identifies current PA, step therapy, pharmacy distribution, and documentation workflows that fragment oncology care.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - The requested API and standards improvements would affect EHR, payer, and interoperability vendors.
